title: Smallest Absent Positive
statement:
You get an unsorted list of integers nums. Return the smallest positive integer (1, 2, 3, …) that does not appear in it.

Your solution must run in O(n) time and use only O(1) extra memory. You may change nums.

examples.why: 1 and 2 are present, 3 is not. The 5 and the negative number do not matter.
1 itself is missing, so it is the answer however large the other values are.
Every value from 1 to n is present, so the answer is n + 1.

hints: With n numbers, the answer is always somewhere in 1 to n + 1. Why?
So only values in 1..n matter. If you could mark "value v is present" for those, the first unmarked value is the answer. A hash set does that with O(n) memory. Where else could the marks live?

Use the array itself: value v belongs at index v − 1. Swap each value into its home until every slot holds its own value or a value that has no home. Then the first index i with nums[i] ≠ i + 1 gives the answer i + 1.

explain.intuition:
n numbers can cover at most the values 1 to n, so the answer is at most n + 1. That means only values between 1 and n are interesting, and there are exactly as many of those possible values as there are slots in the array. The array can serve as its own hash set.

Give each value v a home at index v − 1. Go through the array and keep swapping the current value into its home, as long as it has a home and the home does not already hold it. Every swap puts at least one value where it belongs for good, so the total number of swaps is at most n. Afterwards, walk the array: the first slot whose value is not its own index + 1 tells you which value is missing.
steps: For each index i: while 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ n and nums[nums[i] − 1] ≠ nums[i], swap nums[i] into index nums[i] − 1.
Walk again: return i + 1 for the first i with nums[i] ≠ i + 1.
If every slot is correct, return n + 1.
pitfalls: Checking nums[i] ≠ i + 1 as the loop condition instead of comparing with the home slot. With duplicates like [1, 1] that loops forever.
In Python, writing nums[i], nums[nums[i] - 1] = nums[nums[i] - 1], nums[i]. The left side is assigned in order, so nums[i] changes before the second index is computed. Save the target index first.
Forgetting the n + 1 case when all of 1..n is present.

solutions.title: Hash set
solutions.idea: Put every value in a set, then try 1, 2, 3, … until one is missing. O(n) time, but O(n) extra memory.

solutions.title: Swap every value to its home
solutions.idea: Value v belongs at index v − 1. After placing every value that has a home, the first slot holding the wrong value reveals the answer.

followups: Solve it with sign marking instead of swaps: first replace useless values with n + 1, then mark presence by making nums[v − 1] negative.
Return the k smallest missing positive integers.
